subsection: 13. Advances in military, space and information technology; case study: the Moon landing, 1969

notes.h: Why technology advanced: the Cold War and the military-industrial complex
notes.b: After 1945 the United States and the Soviet Union competed in weapons, space and computing, and governments paid for much of the research. Two key ideas, technological development and the military-industrial complex, tie the whole subject together.
points: Technological development here means the rapid advances in military, space and computing technology after 1945. They were driven largely by Cold War rivalry and by government money, because each superpower feared falling behind the other.

The arms race began after the United States dropped atomic bombs in 1945 and the Soviet Union tested its own atomic bomb in August 1949. Each side then built bigger weapons and better ways of delivering them.

German rocket science mattered too. Wernher von Braun, a German rocket engineer who worked on the V-2 rocket, moved to the United States after 1945 under Operation Paperclip, and he later led the Saturn V work at the Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama.

The military-industrial complex is the alliance of the armed forces, defence contractors (private firms that build weapons and equipment) and politicians. Each gains from high defence spending, so the alliance tends to keep that spending going.

Eisenhower's farewell address on 17 January 1961 warned the nation to guard against the unwarranted influence of the military-industrial complex. Coming from a former general, the warning carried great weight.

In practice the complex funded missiles, aerospace and early computing, and the same research often fed the space and computing programmes. The presidents of the period were Truman, Eisenhower, Kennedy, Johnson, Nixon and Reagan.
notes.tip: For an essay on the military-industrial complex, define it, quote Eisenhower's farewell warning of January 1961, then show it funding missiles, aerospace and computing, and weigh benefits against costs.

notes.h: Nuclear weapons: the decision to build the hydrogen bomb
notes.b: The first atomic bombs were followed by a far more powerful weapon, the hydrogen (thermonuclear) bomb, which uses the fusion of atoms rather than their splitting. The decision to build it was made quickly and not without argument.
points: The Soviet atomic test of August 1949 ended the American monopoly on atomic weapons. This is why pressure grew in the United States to develop something even more powerful.
President Truman announced the decision to develop the hydrogen bomb on 31 January 1950. Edward Teller supported the decision.

J. Robert Oppenheimer and the General Advisory Committee of the Atomic Energy Commission opposed it. Scientists such as Oppenheimer argued the bomb was so destructive that building it would only worsen the arms race.
Ivy Mike, the first American thermonuclear test, took place at Enewetak (Eniwetok) Atoll in the Pacific in November 1952. It showed the United States was ahead.
The Soviet Union tested a hydrogen-bomb type device in August 1953. This was less than a year later, so the United States held its lead only briefly.
notes.tip: Keep the order straight: Soviet atomic test 1949, Truman's decision January 1950, Ivy Mike 1952, Soviet test 1953. Do not call the 1953 Soviet device a thermonuclear weapon without qualification.

notes.h: Delivery systems: bombers, missiles and submarines
notes.b: A bomb is only a threat if it can be delivered. The United States built three ways of delivering nuclear weapons, so that an enemy could not hope to destroy all of them at once.
points: The B-52 Stratofortress, a long-range jet bomber that entered service in 1955, carried nuclear weapons on strategic patrols during the Cold War. Keeping bombers in the air made them hard to destroy on the ground.
Intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs, rockets that carry a warhead from one continent to another) began with the Atlas, operational from about 1959, and then the Minuteman, deployed from 1962.
An ICBM can reach the Soviet Union from the United States in about thirty minutes. This gave the United States the ability to strike very fast and left the Soviets little time to respond.
USS Nautilus, the first nuclear-powered submarine, entered service in 1954. Nuclear power let a submarine stay under water for long periods.

Polaris missiles, fired from submarines, were first carried on patrol in 1960. They gave the United States a second-strike capability (the power to hit back even after being attacked), because hidden submarines could not easily be destroyed in a surprise attack.

By the late 1960s the United States had about 1,000 Minuteman missiles and about 41 Polaris submarines. From about 1970 MIRVs (several warheads on a single missile, first on Minuteman III) multiplied the number of warheads.
MIRVs made arms control more difficult, because each missile now carried several targets' worth of destruction and it was harder to agree how to count and limit the arsenals.
notes.tip: Examiners reward dated examples: B-52 1955, Nautilus 1954, Atlas about 1959, Polaris 1960, Minuteman 1962. Explain what second-strike capability means, not just the name.

notes.h: The missile gap and spy satellites
notes.b: Each side knew little about the other's real strength, and fear filled the gap. Satellites eventually replaced guesswork with photographs.
points: The missile gap was the claim, raised in the late 1950s and by Kennedy in the 1960 election campaign, that the Soviet Union was ahead of the United States in missiles. It made voters fear the nation was falling behind.
In fact the United States held a large lead. American satellite photographs in 1961 showed the Soviet Union had far fewer ICBMs than had been claimed, and the missile gap collapsed.
Before satellites the United States relied on U-2 spy aircraft. In May 1960 the U-2 pilot Gary Powers was shot down over the Soviet Union, which showed how risky such flights were.

The Corona programme (run by the CIA and the US Air Force) took its first successful photographs from space in August 1960. Satellites replaced the risky U-2 flights, so no pilot's life or national embarrassment was at stake.
notes.tip: Do not write that satellites let the US spy without flying over Soviet territory, because satellites do pass over it. The point is that they replaced risky U-2 aircraft flights.

notes.h: The Pentagon as a funder, military spin-offs and the Strategic Defense Initiative
notes.b: Defence spending did not stay in the army and navy. It paid for industries, shaped whole regions and left behind technologies that civilians later used.
points: Jet fighters and bombers, nuclear submarines and guided missiles were funded by the Pentagon (the US Defense Department). Defence contracts supported the aerospace industry in California, Texas and Washington State, which is the military-industrial complex at work.
Military research on computers, radar and jet propulsion created technologies that were later adopted in civil aviation and in commercial electronics, so defence money had civilian benefits.
GPS, the satellite navigation system, began as a military programme, with the first satellite launched in 1978. It shows how a military tool can become an everyday civilian one.
Reagan announced the Strategic Defense Initiative (SDI) in a television address on 23 March 1983. It proposed a space-based defence against missiles, a shield that would destroy them in flight.
Critics nicknamed it 'Star Wars' because it sounded like science fiction. It was never built or deployed, but its research funded lasers and sensors.
notes.tip: A Higher essay pairing SDI with the Moon landing needs the SDI date (23 March 1983), its aim, its critics and its result (never deployed). Link both to the Cold War.

notes.h: The space race begins: Sputnik and the American response
notes.b: On 4 October 1957 the Soviet Union put a small metal sphere into orbit. The United States came to see space as a test of its technological and political strength, and it reacted at once.
points: Sputnik 1, launched on 4 October 1957, was the first artificial satellite (a human-made object that circles the Earth). Sputnik 2, carrying the dog Laika, followed in November 1957.

America's first reply failed publicly: the Vanguard rocket exploded on its launch pad in December 1957. Explorer 1, launched on 31 January 1958 by a team that included von Braun, put the first American satellite into orbit.
Sputnik caused alarm in the United States about Soviet technology and education. A Soviet satellite seemed to show that the rocket that launched it could also carry a nuclear warhead.
The National Defense Education Act of 1958 gave funding for science, mathematics and languages, to produce more engineers and scientists.

NASA, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, was created by Act of 1958, signed by Eisenhower in July and operating from 1 October 1958. It directed the civil space programme and took over work from the military and from the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics.
ARPA, the Pentagon's research agency, was also created in 1958 after Sputnik. It later funded the ARPANET, the network that grew into the internet.
notes.tip: Do not confuse Sputnik (1957, a satellite with no person aboard) with Gagarin's Vostok flight (1961, the first human in space).

notes.b: Both sides raced to put people into space. The Soviets won the early rounds, and each Soviet success increased American pressure to respond.
points: Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space, and the first in orbit, on 12 April 1961. This Soviet achievement increased pressure on the United States to respond.
The Mercury programme of 1958 to 1963 sent the first American astronauts into space. It was designed to find out whether people could survive and work there.
Alan Shepard became the first American in space on 5 May 1961. His flight was suborbital (it rose and fell without circling the Earth) and lasted about fifteen minutes.
John Glenn became the first American to orbit the Earth on 20 February 1962. An orbit means circling the planet, which is much harder than Shepard's up-and-down flight.
The Soviet Union scored further firsts: Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space in June 1963, and Alexei Leonov made the first spacewalk in March 1965.
notes.tip: Do not confuse Shepard's flight (suborbital, 1961) with Glenn's (orbital, 1962), or Sputnik (1957) with Gagarin (1961).

notes.h: Kennedy's pledge, Gemini and the choices for the Moon
notes.b: Kennedy turned the competition into a clear goal with a deadline. The goal then decided how NASA trained, practised and designed its spacecraft.
points: Kennedy's decision followed Gagarin's flight and the failed Bay of Pigs invasion (April 1961). He believed the Moon landing was a field in which the United States could win, because the Soviet Union had a head start with nothing else.
In a speech to Congress on 25 May 1961 Kennedy committed the United States to landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely to Earth before the decade was out.
At Rice University on 12 September 1962 he said the nation chose to go to the Moon, not because it was easy but because it was hard. The speech was meant to win public support for the huge cost.
NASA chose lunar orbit rendezvous in 1962. A separate lunar module descends to the surface while the command module stays in orbit, so only a small craft has to land and take off.
The Gemini programme of 1965 and 1966 practised rendezvous (meeting in space) and docking (joining two craft), as well as long flights. Gemini 8 made the first docking in space in March 1966.
The Soviet Moon rocket, the N1, failed in all four test launches between 1969 and 1972, and the programme was later cancelled. The Soviet crewed lunar effort therefore never reached the Moon.
notes.tip: For Kennedy's commitment give the date (25 May 1961), the reasons (Gagarin, the Bay of Pigs, Cold War prestige) and the Rice University speech of 1962.

notes.h: Case study: how Apollo was organised and paid for
notes.b: The Apollo programme was the largest peacetime technological effort the United States had undertaken. Reaching the Moon depended as much on organisation and money as on rockets.
points: NASA managed Apollo with major contractors: North American Aviation (command and service modules and the second stage), Grumman (lunar module), Boeing (first stage of the Saturn V) and IBM. It employed hundreds of thousands of people across the country.
James Webb, NASA administrator from 1961, managed the political side and the vast contracting system. He had to keep Congress and industry committed over many years.

Each centre had its own job: the Marshall Space Flight Center in Alabama built rockets under von Braun, the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston, Texas, directed flights, and Kennedy Space Center in Florida launched them.
Universities took part too. The Apollo Guidance Computer was developed at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
Employment was concentrated in Florida, Texas, Alabama and California, which tied the growth of the Sun Belt (the southern and western states) to federal spending.
Apollo cost about 25 billion dollars in the money of its time. NASA's share of federal spending peaked in the mid-1960s at about 4 to 5 per cent, which shows the scale of the commitment.
Critics attacked the cost. Amitai Etzioni's The Moon-Doggle (1964) called the programme a waste, and some in Congress argued that the money would be better spent on poverty.
notes.tip: Say 'hundreds of thousands' for the workforce and 'about 4 to 5 per cent' for the budget peak, in the mid-1960s. Marks go to named organisations, the cost and scale.

notes.h: Case study: the hardware, setbacks and testing before Apollo 11
notes.b: A Moon landing needed a giant rocket, a three-part spacecraft and a series of tests, some of them tragic. Each mission tested one more step of the plan.
points: The Saturn V was a three-stage rocket about 110 metres tall and the most powerful rocket built to that time. It flew thirteen times, and none of its flights lost a crew.

The Apollo spacecraft had three parts: the command module, which carried the crew back to Earth, the service module, which supplied power and propulsion, and the lunar module, which took two astronauts to the surface.
The Apollo Guidance Computer was one of the first computers to use integrated circuits (many tiny electronic parts on one chip). This made the programme a major customer for the new technology.

The Apollo 1 fire on 27 January 1967, in the capsule during a test on the launch pad, killed Gus Grissom, Ed White and Roger Chaffee. It led to a redesign of the spacecraft, so later crews were safer.

Apollo 7 (October 1968) tested the command module in Earth orbit. Apollo 8, 21 to 27 December 1968, carried Frank Borman, Jim Lovell and William Anders as the first humans to orbit the Moon, though not to land.
Apollo 8 returned the Earthrise photograph, which showed the Earth rising over the lunar horizon.
In 1969 Apollo 9 (March) tested the lunar module in Earth orbit, and Apollo 10 (May) flew the lunar module to about 15 kilometres above the surface without landing.
notes.tip: Keep the missions apart: Apollo 8 orbited the Moon but did not land, Apollo 10 flew near the surface without landing, Apollo 11 was the first landing. Do not confuse the Apollo 1 fire (1967) with Challenger (1986).

notes.h: Case study: Apollo 11 from launch to splashdown
notes.b: Apollo 11 was launched from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida, landed in the Sea of Tranquillity and returned its crew to the Pacific. The mission can be told in order of dates.
points: The crew were Neil Armstrong (commander), Edwin 'Buzz' Aldrin (lunar module pilot) and Michael Collins (command module pilot), who stayed in orbit around the Moon in Columbia. Collins did not walk on the Moon.
Apollo 11 was launched on 16 July 1969 on a Saturn V from Kennedy Space Center, and it entered lunar orbit on 19 July.

The lunar module Eagle landed in the Sea of Tranquillity on 20 July 1969. The landing was risky: computer alarms sounded during the descent, and Armstrong took manual control to avoid a field of boulders.
Eagle landed with very little fuel left, so the margin for error had been small.
Armstrong stepped onto the surface late that evening, at 10.56 pm Eastern time. Aldrin joined him, so Armstrong was first and Aldrin second, and the two spent about two and a half hours outside.
The crew collected about 21 kilograms of lunar rock and soil, and left scientific instruments behind, including a seismometer that measured the Moon's seismic activity.
Apollo 11 splashed down in the Pacific Ocean on 24 July 1969, and the USS Hornet picked up the crew. They then spent about three weeks in quarantine in case they carried lunar germs.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level questions reward four or five dated facts on one stage, such as launch, landing and return: 16 July, 19 July, 20 July, 24 July, crew, landing site.

notes.h: Case study: the words, the plaque, the television audience and the Soviet reaction
notes.b: The landing was as much a public event as a technical one. What was said and left on the Moon, and who watched, shaped how it was understood.
points: Armstrong's first words on the Moon are remembered as 'one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind'. He said he intended to say 'a man', but the 'a' is not clearly audible, so it is safest not to claim he definitely said or omitted it.

The crew left a plaque reading 'We came in peace for all mankind' and planted an American flag. They did not claim the Moon for the United States, because the Outer Space Treaty of 1967 forbids national claims to the Moon.

The landing was broadcast live on television around the world. Estimates of the audience run from about 500 to 600 million, so it is safest to say hundreds of millions, which made it one of the most watched events in history.
President Nixon spoke to the astronauts by telephone from the White House. This allowed the President to share in the national triumph.
The Soviet Union's Luna 15, a robot probe, crashed on the Moon on 21 July 1969, while Apollo 11 was on the surface, as it tried to return samples. Soviet media played down the Apollo achievement.
notes.tip: Name Armstrong's words carefully and do not state flatly whether he said 'a'. A short answer on a photograph or press report should say who was involved, the year and why it mattered to the US.

notes.h: Case study: significance at home and abroad
notes.b: The landing answered Sputnik and Gagarin, but not everyone at home thought it was worth the price. Its meaning differed between the United States, the world and the critics.
points: At home the landing brought national pride. It fulfilled Kennedy's pledge of 1961 and was a tribute to American technology and organisation.
Abroad it was a Cold War victory for the United States over the Soviet Union. It showed technological leadership, and it became an image of American technology for the rest of the world.
The Soviet reaction was to play down the achievement. After the N1 failures the Soviet Union had no way of answering.
The triumph contrasted with the troubled society of 1969, when the nation was divided by Vietnam, urban unrest and protest. Some commentators saw the cost as a diversion from poverty.
Gil Scott-Heron's poem 'Whitey on the Moon' (1970) is a well-known protest at the spending on the Moon while poverty continued.
notes.tip: Split significance into national (pride, technology), international (Cold War victory, prestige) and limits (cost, declining interest). Do not treat the landing as ending the space race at once.

notes.h: Later Apollo missions and declining interest
notes.b: Once the race was won, the reason for the spending weakened. Public interest and political support fell, and the programme was cut back.
points: Apollo 12 (November 1969), 14, 15, 16 and 17 landed on the Moon, making five further landings after Apollo 11. The last, Apollo 17 in December 1972, was the last Apollo Moon landing.

Apollo 13 (April 1970) was crippled by an oxygen tank explosion and the crew returned safely without landing. It was praised as a triumph of engineering and teamwork, but it also made the public aware of the risks.
Apollo flights 18 to 20 were cancelled. Public interest and political support declined after 1969, and NASA's budget fell in the early 1970s, so the cuts were a result of the race having been won.
Skylab, the first American space station, was launched in May 1973. The Apollo-Soyuz mission of July 1975 was the first joint US-Soviet crewed flight, a sign of easing rivalry.
notes.tip: Do not say that Apollo 13 landed: it never did. Say instead that the last Apollo Moon landing was in December 1972.

notes.h: The Space Shuttle and the Challenger disaster
notes.b: After Apollo, NASA turned to a reusable spacecraft. The Shuttle was meant to make space cheap and routine, but its second decade ended in disaster.
points: The Space Shuttle Columbia made the first Shuttle flight on 12 April 1981. It was intended to make access to space routine and cheaper, because the craft could be used again.
Challenger broke up 73 seconds after launch on 28 January 1986, killing all seven crew members. Among them was the schoolteacher Christa McAuliffe.
The cause was the failure of an O-ring seal in a solid rocket booster in cold weather. The seal let hot gas escape.
The Rogers Commission of 1986 also criticised NASA's decision-making, which shows the disaster was a management failure as well as an engineering one.
notes.tip: Do not confuse Challenger (1986, Shuttle, in flight) with Apollo 1 (1967, fire on the ground) or Apollo 13 (1970, survived). The Challenger disaster is used to show management failures.

notes.h: Information technology: from ENIAC to the microprocessor
notes.b: Computing grew from room-sized wartime machines into small, cheap devices. Each step made computers smaller and faster, and the steps are best learned as a dated chain.
points: ENIAC was completed in 1945 at the University of Pennsylvania and unveiled in February 1946. It was one of the first general-purpose electronic computers, built to calculate artillery firing tables for the US Army.
UNIVAC was delivered to the US Census Bureau in 1951 as the first commercial computer in the United States. CBS used one on election night 1952 to predict the presidential election.
The transistor, invented at Bell Laboratories in 1947, replaced the vacuum tube (a bulky glass switch). It made computers smaller, faster and more reliable.

IBM's System/360, launched in 1964, was a family of compatible computers (programs could run on any model). It set a standard for business computers and made IBM the dominant computer firm of the period.
The integrated circuit placed many transistors on a single chip. Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments (1958) and Robert Noyce at Fairchild (1959) developed it independently.
Gordon Moore observed in 1965 that the number of components on a chip doubled roughly every year, later put at about every two years. It became a guide to the industry's growth.
Intel's 4004, released in 1971, was the first commercial microprocessor, putting a complete central processing unit (the part that does the computing) on a single chip.
notes.tip: Answers earn marks for a chain of dated advances: ENIAC 1946, transistor 1947, integrated circuit 1958 to 1959, microprocessor 1971. Do not confuse the integrated circuit with the microprocessor, or the transistor with the vacuum tube.

notes.h: ARPANET, personal computers and Silicon Valley
notes.b: Computers moved from the Pentagon and universities into homes and offices. Defence money and the space programme were the early customers that made this possible.
points: ARPANET, funded by ARPA of the Defense Department, was a network of computers. Its first message, sent on 29 October 1969, travelled from the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) to the Stanford Research Institute.

Apple's Apple II (1977) and the IBM Personal Computer (1981) brought computing into homes and offices. The IBM PC used an operating system supplied by Microsoft, which made Microsoft the dominant software firm.
Apple's Macintosh of 1984 popularised the graphical interface, which let users click on pictures instead of typing commands.

Silicon Valley (the Santa Clara Valley in California, south of San Francisco) grew around Stanford University and firms such as Hewlett-Packard, Fairchild Semiconductor and Intel, helped by defence contracts and university research.

Early chips were bought by the US military and by NASA for missiles and the Apollo computer. These customers paid high prices, which let the firms improve chips until they became cheap enough for the public.
The three fields fed one another: defence money and the space race created demand for small, light electronics, and computing in turn helped missiles and spacecraft.
notes.tip: Link information technology to defence funding and Silicon Valley, with dates: ARPANET 1969, Apple II 1977, IBM PC 1981.

notes.b: Space and military research produced satellites that transformed communications and weather forecasting. Their civilian uses became a justification for the programmes.
points: TIROS 1, launched on 1 April 1960, was the first successful weather satellite. It sent back television images of cloud cover.
Telstar, launched on 10 July 1962, was the first active communications satellite. The first public live transatlantic television broadcasts followed on 23 July 1962.
The Communications Satellite Act of 1962 created the Communications Satellite Corporation (COMSAT), a private-public body that set up the Intelsat global satellite system.

Space technology also contributed to the miniaturisation of electronics, computer memory and materials. Historians debate how large these spin-offs were, because some of the advances would have happened anyway.
notes.tip: Do not give 10 July 1962 as the date live television crossed the Atlantic. That was Telstar's launch; the first public broadcasts were on 23 July 1962.

notes.h: Assessment: was the Moon landing worth its cost?
notes.b: Examiners reward judgements that weigh the achievements of the programme against its limits, and that compare how contemporaries and later historians saw it.
points: Achievement: the landing was a triumph of American engineering and organisation, achieved within the decade Kennedy had set. It was also a Cold War victory over the Soviet Union.
Limit: the cost was enormous, about 25 billion dollars. Critics argued the programme was driven by rivalry with the Soviet Union rather than by scientific need.
Achievement: it left lasting technologies, such as satellites and computing, that inspired advances in materials and medicine.
Limit: interest and budgets fell once the race was won, and the Challenger disaster exposed management failures in NASA.
Contemporaries celebrated the landing as a national and global achievement. Critics on the left and in Congress saw the cost as a diversion from poverty and urban problems.

Later historians stress the Cold War motive and regard Apollo as a short burst of spending, shown by the lack of follow-up missions. They also stress its lasting technological legacy in computing and satellites.
notes.tip: A Higher answer needs a clear thesis, then strands on the political commitment, organisation and resources, and outcome, with a judgement. Describing the landing without explaining why the US wanted it loses marks.

keyTerms.definition: The advances in military, space and computing technology after 1945, such as the thermonuclear bomb, the Apollo spacecraft and the microprocessor, which shaped the Cold War.
The network of defence contractors, military officers and politicians whose shared interests promoted technological and defence spending, including the space and missile programmes.
The intercontinental ballistic missile, a long-range nuclear-armed rocket, which the United States deployed from 1959, including the Atlas and the Minuteman.
A set of transistors and other components built on a single chip of semiconductor material, developed independently by Kilby and Noyce in 1958 and 1959.
A chip that contains the central processing unit of a computer, first released by Intel in 1971.
The competition between the United States and the Soviet Union to achieve milestones in space, from Sputnik in 1957 to the Moon landing in 1969.
NASA's programme of crewed missions to the Moon from 1967 to 1972, which culminated in the first landing in July 1969.
The Defense Department's early computer network, which sent its first message between UCLA and the Stanford Research Institute in October 1969.
The three-stage rocket designed under Wernher von Braun that launched the Apollo Moon missions.
The method chosen in 1962 for the Moon landing, in which a small lunar module descends to the surface while the command module stays in lunar orbit.
